St. Croix Ciikistiansted, Thursday Oct'br. 22, 1840 The second September mail from England reached yesterday, All eyes are turned to us the East þÿ the theatre of the approaching war. The Pacha of Egypt rejects all offers made him by the allies. The Agents of the Four Powers at Alexandria have had their last audience of leave. Colonel Hodges the British Consul General on remonstrating with the Pacha on the risks he incurred, was answered very haughtily by Mehemet Ali w ho expressed at being annoyed in that manner. The Four agents Englund, Russia, Austria ol and Prussia immediately left his presence. The blockade of the Egyptian and Syrian coasts was to commence in ten days. Admiral Stopford with a part of his fleet, in conjunction with an Austrian Squadron was before Alexandria, and Commodore Napier with another part of the fleet, was at St. Jean d'Acre and Beyroot in Syria, and had issued a proclamation to the inhabitants of Mount Lebanon assuring them of the support and protection of the allies against their oppressor.

Mehemet Ali had informed Admiral Stopford that he might commence his operations as soon as he pleased, as he did not wish to avail himself of the lime allowed by the allies. The French Government had notified the Pacha that they should offer him no armed support against the allies. It was thought that one of the first operations of Admiral Stopford would be to attempt the destruction of the Egyptian fleet at Alexandria. A combined army of 25.0U0 Turks, Austrians and English were to land in Syria. Ibrahim Bey had a powerful army there of 112,000 men, besides as many more in Egypt under Mehemet Ali. Solyinan Bey (formerly the French renegade Colonel Sieves) commanded a large corps of Ibrahim's army at Beyroot and St. Jean d'Acre, and would be the first to come in contact wuh the allies '1 he Bnttania 120, the Royal Adelaide 120 and the Howe 120 were nearly yeady for Sea at Portsmouth, waiting to complete their crews, and the Vanguard 80 with the 1.9th regiment on board, were all to sail soon to reinforce Admiral Stopford, and the Augsburg gazette states that a Russian fleet of 18 ships of war bad received orders to sail from the Bal tc for the Mediterranean lor the same purpose, thus placing under Admiral Slopfords command 40 ships of the line. Several large war Steamers were ordered to leave England with troops, ammunition &c. for the same destination.

RUSSIA. PRUSSIA, AND AUSTRIA. We hear from the North east (say the Prussians) of nothing hut warlike preparations and marching of troops in Russia, partly towards Asia Minor, partly towards Circassia. Notwithstanding all the official and unofficial accounts of the French, no orders have yet been given here (at Berlin) for any such preparations on our part. Nor is any uneasiness felt on that account ; for (say the writers on the subject) on the one hand, we know that no great preparation or loss of time is required to have our reserve and the Eandwehr completely armed ; and, on the other hand, the outcry of the Paris journals is estimated at its own value, and no more. The Saxon papers announce the arrival of the King of Prussia at Pillnitz, where he was met by Prince Metternich, Count Fiquelinont, Counts Malszahn and Nesselrode, and other statesmen of note. On the 29th instant the King is to arrive at Konigsberg, to receive the homage of East Prussia General Count OrlofF has been appointed by the Emperor Nicholas to the Post of commander in chief of the armies now collected in the southern provinces ot the Russian empire and on the shores of the Black Sea. The French Ambassador at St. Petersburgh M de Bararite, is to be recalled, and a simple Charge d'Alfuires, M. Casimir Perior, late secretary to the embassy at Naples> is to be substituted lor him. Baron de Brunow, Russian Ambassador at the Court of London, has received the following Imperial rescript, dated Peterhofl, the 30th of last mouth : þÿ

The very able execution of several important missions which we have confided to you, and the happy result of them, have called our especial attention to you. As a testimony of 1, En mellem Isaac Haiitmann op Chri- j our satisfaction and our gratitude for these services, we have been pleased to confer on you our Imperial order of the While Eagle, the insignia of which you receive herewith, and which you will wear according to the regulations. We remain, &c. Nicholas. The King of Prussia, in his desire to make the amnesty appear the work of his father instead of his own, has published it before the ceremony of receiving homage at Konigsberg. where it was expected to have been issued.

It appears that King Leopold of Belgium, who lately paid a visit to Queen Victoria, and returned again to the Continent, on the tilth nl August, has received a commission from the Emperor of Austria to use his good offices with Louis Philippe for the preservation of peace ; at least we read that while in England he gave audience to M. Guizot, the French Ambassador, immediately after his return from France, and also to Baron de Nieumann, on a special mission from the Emperor of Austria. The Paiis correspondent of the Times says that letters have been received in that capital from the French Embassy in London, which announce positively that matters have taken a sudden and favorable turn, owing to the unremitting exertions ot the King of the Belgians. They farther state that Leopold will proceed to the Rhine, to follow up his negotiations.

The Capitole mentions a report in the political circles that M. Guizot had succeeded, throu"h the intervention of the King of the Belgians, in arranging the misunderstanding which had occurred between the courts of London and Paris in consequence of the treaty of the 15th July.

TURKEY AND EGYPT. On the arrival at Alexandria of the news that the treaty ot London was signed, the French Consul called on the Pacha and persuaded him to yield. Mehemet Ali declared to M. Cochlet that, under existing circumstances, he could not think ol giving up the Ottoman fleet ; that he confided in Providence, and would leave it to decide on his destinies and those of his family. The general opinion in Turkey is, that on the first energetic notification made by the great, powers to Mehemet Ali, Ibrahim 1 acha will march to Constantinople ; every one is convinced that such is Mehemet Ali s intention. It agrees with the advice which .he has received from his friends at Constantinople.

A private correspondent of the Times writes, under date of Paris, Wednesday evening, to the following effect : þÿ " 1 think it ri"ht O to inform " you, without loss ot time, that letters received l&st night from the French embassy in London, although in a private form, announce positively that matters have just taken a sudden and favourable turn (that is, of a pacific nature) owing to the unremitting exertions of King Leopold cf Belgium." The Archimedes, Patent Screw-propeller Ship. þÿ This vessel made the voyage from Plymouth to Oporto in 70 hours, and, on Wednesday morning, intelligence was received of her return from Oporto to Plymouth in 88 hours, total out and home 157 hours, the must part of which was performed against strong head winds and a heavy sea. This is unquestionably the most successful voyage ever made by a steam vessel, the efficient working power of which has been ascertained not to exceed 65 horses, and we imagine there can no longer be any question as to the superiority of patent screw propellers as Compared with paddle wheels. þÿ Sun.

We answer, to a variety of causes, but chiefly to the gross mismanagement of the planters themselves- Instead of at once endeavouring to secure the confidence of the people, by kind and generous treatment by þÿ encouraging thorn to settle down in their respective localities on fair and equitable terms þÿ and by offers of liberal, or at all events, adequate remuneration for their labour, they commenced with a system of irritation and annoyance, as though it were their deliberate intention to alienate the affections of the people ; þÿ they sought to keep them dow n in a state of abject subjection, by attempting to exercise direct control over their domestic circumstances þÿ by threats (in multitudes of instances enforced) of summary ejectment from their domiciles þÿ by the imposition of enormous and unlawful rents upon every member of a family occupying one and the same tenement þÿ by raising such rents at the caprice of the employer, as the means of enforcing compliance with his selfish demands by the destination of the provision grounds of the labourer by impounding his stock, þÿ and abusing, insulting, and calumniating him, both in public and þÿprivate and finally by attempting to take advantage of his ignorance, and helplessness, by the offer of wages which he knew to be iufinitely below the value of his labour.

These circumstances combined produced an amount of discontent, distrust, and suspicion which will account for a large share of that want of steady and continuous industry of wnich such complaint bad been made. These however are by no means the only causes of the falling off there is one, which þÿ has been little dwelt on, and yet it has had powerful influence in producing the disastrous results. We allude to the irregular and uncertain payments of wages. In some cases such irregularity proceeds from sheer poverty, in others, payments are capriciously delayed until the wages have accumulated, and then, on a variety of pretexts, unjust and vexatious deductions are made, which lead to contention and litigation, and frequently desertion from labour." þÿ Colonial Reformer, August 15.

From the New York Commercial Advertiser, September 10, 1840. Perils of the Sea. þÿ The following is an extract from a letter written by an officer on boaid the Peacock, (one of the exploring squadron,) and published in the National Intelligencer. " Sidney, New South Wades, " A arch 16. 1840. " Before this reaches you, you will probably have heard of our return to this port for repairs, having been compelled to do so by injuries received in the ice, by which we were confined for forty most anxious hours þÿ for twenty hours with the imminent fear of most awful death. So closely was the ice packed around us, and in such vast masses, that even undr a press of canvass, assisted by ice anchors and every other means that expeiience or necessity could suggest, we at tunes remained motionless lbr hours þÿ the ice cutting into the vitals of the ship, and threatening to grind us to powder. "On the evening of þÿthe (date forgotten, and, being now in town, cannot refer) þÿ having procured soundings and seen appearances of land, cheered with the prospect of reaching it, we worked in through heavy drill ice ; and next morning, about 9 A. M" in endeavoring to avoid a large mass ahead, we gave her a sternboard, which almost instantly brought the rudder in contact with another mass, and, so violent was the shock' that the rudder-head was wrenched off, and the rudder fixed immovably athwart ships, rendering the ship almost entirely unmanageable. We used every effort to wear her, but, like mad, she drove on through the ice, till it became so close as to be impassable.

We then furled sails, planted ice anchors, and resolved to lie quiet tiil we could repair our rudder, when suddenly a large body of ice under our stern shifted its position, the anchors came home, and we drove down on a range of icebergs masthead high, and over hanging the decks, and with breathless anxiety awaited the shock, (which nothing humane could prevent) þÿ an immense impending mass tottering to its fall, and threatening to crush us beneath it. Our spanker boom struggled for a moment, and then broke like a reed ; the stern-boat crushed like an eggshell ; and then went stern davits and all the upper works on the starboard side, as far as the gangway þÿ every stanchion broken short off. The ship rebounded I We breathed again, and hauled aft jib and staysail sheets and gave her a cant off from our inhospitable neighbor. We then made sail, and, by great exertions, had a most providential escape, after thumping off our forefoot, and cutting into the stern within an inch and a half of the 'woodeods,' or (in as good English) within an inch and a half of our lives. Had our confinement been prolonged another hour, we should all have gone to Davy Jones. "1 have mentioned the anxiety with which we viewed the overhanging mass loitering to its fall. As soon as a sufficient space had intervened between our stern and the iceberg, it fell ! harmlessly in our wake."

i Bonaparte's a Wounds. Napoleon showed me the marks of two wounds þÿ one a very deep cicatrice above the left knee, which he said he had received in his first campaign of Italy, and it was of so serious a nature, that the surgeons were in doubt whether it might not be ultimately necessary to amputate. He observed, that when he was wounded it was always kept a secret in order not to discourage the soldier. 1 he other was on the toe, and had been received at Eckmuhi. " At the siege of Acre," continued he, " a shell thrown by Sidney Smith fell at my feet. Two soldiers, who were close by, seized, and closely embraced me, one in front and the other on one side, and made a rampart of their bodies for me against the effect of the shell, which exploded, and overwhelmed us with sand. We sunk into the whole formed by its bursting ; one of them was wounded. I made them both officers. One has since lost a leg at Moscow and commanded at Vincennes when 1 left Paris. When jhe was summoned bv the liussians, he replied, that as soon as they sent him back the leg he had lost at Moscow, he would surrender the fortress " Many times in my life, continued he, " have I been saved by soldiers and officers throwing themselves before me when 1 was in the most imminent danger. At Areola, when I was advancing, Colonel Meuran, my aid-de camp, threw himself before me, covered me witfi his bodv, and received the wound which was destined for me. lie fell at my feet, and his blood spouted up iu my face He gave his life to pre-

serve mine. Never yet, I believe, has there been such devotion shown by soldiers as mine have manifested for me. In all my misfortunes, ne-er has the soldier, even when expiring, been wanting to me þÿ never has man been served more faithfully by his troops þÿ With the last drop of blood gushing out of their veins, they exclaimed ' Vive I'Empereur !' "--From " A Voice from St. Helena."

Thunder Storm þÿ Mine Persona Killed. Woodstock, (S. C.) July 20.- A dreadful thunder storm passed over this section of country, on Friday evening, the 17th inst., in which there was an awful destruction of I human life. Just previous to its bursting upon ihem, twenty of the negroes belonging to the Hon Henry Middlelon, being crowded into a house, whither they had repaired as a place of refuge, were struck down by a vivid flash of lightning, and the following is the result of the stroke. Four of them escaped entirely þÿ two were severely shocked þÿ five were stunned, and nine were killed upon the spot. The electric fluid entered the house at the door, carrying part of the side of the house and gable, and after doing some other damage, seemed to separate into diflerent fragments, as each alternate individual was killed or wounded þÿ it then left the house at the back door, and in its passage killed two of the people five paces from the house, into which they were hastening. The nine who were killed never moved nor manifested any signs of animation, bul presented a heap of mangled corpses. The live who were stunned recovered their senses only after the expiration of an hour, and two who were only severely shocked did not lose their recollection. The

r jrwvisible and external marks were different according to the intensity of the stroke upon each Those who were stu med were and are very much swollen and puffed up, especially in the extremities; but how shall I describe the appearance of those who were killed, nine inanimate beings, who but a few hours before stood up in all the vigor of life, now lay riven and blasted by the dreadful thunder bolt, their features and bodies bloated and swollen to the full extent of the skin, was so disfigured as nearly to obliterate the identity of the individual, the blood uncoagulated poured from their noses and ears, the muscles, as is usual, so entirely relaxed, as to peimit the body to be fixed in any direction. In two only of these was their any abraison of the skin, and that slight, extending merely to the cuticle þÿ Correspondence Charleston Mercury.

Remarkable Instance op Canine Sagacity. þÿ A gentleman of property had a mastiff of great size, very watchful, and altogether, a fine, intelligent animal. Though often let out to range about, he was in general chained up during the day in a wooden house, constructed for his comfort and shelter. On a certain day, when let out. he was observed to attach himself particularly to his master; and when the servant, as usual, came to tie him up. he clung so to his master's feet þÿ showed such anger when they attempted'to force him away, and altogether was so particular in his manner, that the gentleman desired him to be left as he was, and with him he continued the whole day : and when night came on, still he staid by him. and on going towards his bed, room, the dog resolutely, and for the first time in his life, went up a long with him, and rushing into the room, took refuge under the bed, from whence neither blows nor caresses could draw Itim. In the middle of the night a man burst into the room, and, dagger in hand, attempted to stab the sleeping gentleman ; but the dog darted at the robber's neck, fastened his fangs in him, and so kept him down that his master had time to c all for assistance and secure the ruffian, who turned out to he the coachman, and who afterwards confessed, that seeing his master receive a large sum of money, he and the groom conspired together to rob and murder him þÿ and that they plotted their whole scheme leaning over the roof of' the dog's house ! þÿ Dublin Magazine.

For this purpose be bought some anatomical plates of the heart, and com pored them with his own body, in order to .ascertain the exact situation of that organ. On his arrival in France, Bonaparte ordered that fie should remain at Bennes, and not proceed to Paris. Villeneuve, afraid of being tried bv a court martial for disobedience of orders, amf: consequently losing his fleet, (for N.i|dcnft had ordered him not to sail or to engage tVe English.) determined to destroy himself; and accordingly took Ins plates and compared them with the position of ins heart. Exactly in the centre he made a mark with a large pin ; then fixed it, as near as he could judge, in t fie same spot iu his own breast, and shoved it on to its head ; it partial. :d his heart, Bt.d lie expired When the room was ottetied, ire was found dead, the pin through his breast, and a mark in the plate corresponding wu)i the wound. þÿ The Anatomn of Suicide,

COMMUNICATION The termination of what is usually called the Hurricane season in the West Indies under such auspicious circumstances as we now witness, gives rise to renewed motives o' gratitude towards the Great Giver of all good. Th highly favorable weather for the growth and advancement of the Cane which our Island has experienced during the months of Septembei and October, and which have so completely changed the dreary prospect winch tlueatened us iri the preceeding month8 with a total loss of Crop, is indeed a source ol gratulation to all interested in the pmsperi" ty of Santa Cruz; and although there are small portions of our Island which the drought tint prevailed during the spring and summer months have deprived of the hope of making b ;t little produce, yet in general, the present prospect, united with a continuance of good weather lor the next three months, will doubtless insure to the other portions of the Island a saving crop. It is also a source of grateful reminiscence that all our sister Islands have escaped this year the devastating etfecis of the Hurricane while other parts ot :he world have been visited with destruc tive Tornados, Earthquakes, Storms, and ' moving accidents" by Hood and field. Rut it does not become us to claim anv merit as recipients of these marks of the favor of the Almighty. þÿ We are told that "He sendeth his rain equally on the just and the unjust" þÿ were we to be recompensed in this world according to our merits we much fear that we should receive very few n.aiks of

Di vine favor ; and although we know that the Almighty " does not w illingly afflict the children of men." we also learn from the same divine source that the troubles which befall us in this world, are intended fur our good and aie particular Iv manifested towards those "whom the Lord loveth " This truth should prove a great consolation to the children of adversity, and far repay them for the loss ol worldly þÿprosperity. But " let us not d.spiso the chasienings of the Eord" and if these trials do not have the effect of softening our stoney hearts and drawing us to the paths which lead to life eternal, then indeed, they are lost upon us; and "what does He require of thee Oh I man, but to do justly, to Jove mercy and to walk humbly with thy God." I'lie great goodness of our Heavenly Father towards lire guilty race of Adam manifested in sending his only beloved Son into the World to save sinners, and to proclaim salvation and forgiveness of sins through faith in ins blood, is indeed glad tidings of great Joy to criminals under sentence of condemnation (lor such were we arid such we shall he it we wilfully reject the preferred offer of grace.) To such it may be well to consider that " There is no other nome given under Heaven among men by which we can be saved," that a reliance on our own merits is hut to trust to a broken staff and that intercession at the throne of grace in any other name but that of Jesus Christ, can fie of no avail, and that invocations and prayers addressed to

other persons except the Deity, as intercessors are but a return to Paganism and gross idolatry utterly opposed to the truth and to faith in Jesus Christ. It is a remarkable characteristic of Christianity that it war's not with Human systems of Government, that it teaches " to render unto Cesar the things which are Cesar's and to <Jud the things which are God's," and "to be

in subjection to the powers that be as ordained of God" and that it adapts itself to all states of society. Under whatever oppression or injustice we labor, it teaches submission and patience to put our trust in God for relief, knowing that wherever the Heavenly precept prevails that "whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them" that there the hand of the oppressor will be stayed; this divine precept is addressed to all men without distinction. Among the many corruptions of Christianity which now exist in the world, that of Christians still adhering to the exactions of the Jewish law in regard to the sabbath is to be remarked as a prominent one. Either Chris tians should keep the seventh day of the week in the rigid manner prescribed by the law, or they should keep he first day of the week as was done by the fiist Christians ; the talk of " desecrating the sabbath is now inconsistent and not warranted under the Christian dispensation. We cannot forget that our Saviour was charged by the Priests and Pharisees of his day with " desecrating the sabbath," because he healed the sick on that day and walked through the fields of corn plucking the ears as he went His severe rebuke to them for their hypocrisy on that occasion caunpt be forgot. The institution ot the Sabbath (or day of rest) is of heavenly origin, and a strong proof of the wisdom of the Almighty That the laboring man worn down by- the incessant work of six days, required the seventh to res-

tore and renew his strength, 110 man of feeling or hu nanity will deny, and the advantages ot the cessation from labor on that day are too strongly felt not to be properly appreciated bv the laboring classes, a and however the pampered sons of pride and luxury may esteem it, yet it may well be questioned if by any change of destiny they were doomed to labor, if they would not hail with jov the return of the day of rest and wish for it long before the six days find expired. '1 lie command to cease from labour on the seventh day was as much given out of consideration for the health of the laborer, as intended as a check to his propensity of overworking himself for pecuniary inducements, As regards the practices of the first Christians relative to keeping the Jewish Sabbath, we know that those brought up under the Jewish Law adhered to the law, and so lliey did with regard to circumcision &c ; but no sucli observances were enjoined by the Gentiles, converted to Christianity, (from whom we are descended ) On the contrary, the Apostle Paul declares that the observance of lite Jewish ordnances, were not required of them tun only such as he specifics. The first Christians were in the habit of assembling on the first day of the week tn the evening to commemorate the resurrection and to pattake of the Lord's supper, but there is no evidence to show that hey did not attend to their occupations (for they were laboring men) during the rest of the day. The observance by Christians of the first day of the week

should be kept according to the practice of the primitive church and if the day is devoted to religious instruction and to the study of the Scriptures, so much the better. It at least, will recall lis from worldly pursuits for one day in the week, and lead us to reflect on our future state, and enlighten our minds in the attainment of eternal salvation. But the Christian dispensation superceded the Jewish Law with its ceremonies, sacrifi-

mrm ces and observances. Christ fulfilled that law and by the Great sacrifice he made on the cross for sin, H e finished the uoik given him to do, and no farther sacrifices were required of his followers. lie is their great High Priest now ascended into Heaven to make intercession for sinners, having already made atonement for all those who believe on His name and in His power to save to the uttermost. No earthly order of Pr iesthood was established by Him, nor enjoined by his followers þÿ the Apostles. The organisation of the first christian church was simply by the appointment of two eldets to preside at their meeting, and of Deacons to attend to their pecuniary concerns ; afterwards the apostles appointed Bishops, generally young men educated for the ministry, to prearh Arc. The name is derived from the Greek word " Episcopos," a very humble office in its origin, and assimilating with that of shepherd or pastor, but not equal in authority to the elders, One great object of the Chrisiian dispensation was to manifest to the Jews, how far, by the observance of mere forms and ceremonies, and by substituting the traditions of men, for the law as given bv Moses, they had departed from and made void the law, and overlooked the gieat principles of justice, mercy and truth therein inculcated In the same way modern Christianity lias been corrupted by leaving the plain, simple practices of Christ anil the Apostles & following a the traditions of men. The severe rebukes given bv our

Saviour to the Priests and Pharisees of his time for their gross hypocrisy in prever'.ing the truth might well apply to tnanv professors of Christianity of our times. The corruptions of religion have probably occasioned much of the infidelity so prevalent in the world ; may the day soon arrive ' when the knowledge of the Lord shall cover the earth as the waters cover the sea," and when the command of our Saviour to his followers, the appeal to every man's conscience, comprised in these words, " whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ve also to them," may be universally practiced. In conclusion, when reflecting on the causes we possess of grateful recollection, we should not forget that our Island is in the enjoyment of great, quiet and perfectly free from civil commotions, and perhaps not a spot on this habitable globe is more tranquil than Santa Cruz. Our laboring population go through their duties cheerfully, and thanks to the pains taken by our Governor General to prevent cruel acts of oppression on tbc Estates, and to see that the laboring classes are duly protected by the Government þÿ little cause of complaint now exists ; the measures now in contemplation to educate and christianise our Peasantry, and to ameliorate their condition w ill still farther tend to their improvement and to the general prosperity of the Island. s - 1 . 1 1 ' ' a t Advertisements vvi'l he irceived at the ollire a of litis Unj er until 10 o'clock 011 Mondays and '1 liiirsdav s.

The ordinance of the 11th Novb. 1770, 1 0th July 1778, 13th April 1779, 10th March 1792, and the 1st October 1802, together with the governor general's placard of the 10th Nov. 1823, with the exception of the instalments for paying the capitation tax, ha>e laid down the manner in which payment of taxes on properties in the westiudies arc to be paid and the following rules are to be observed: That Negroes wilfully not given up by their owners or by those persons in whose possession they are, will be sold for account ol the king, and the informer, if any. The capitation tax to the royal treasury is 40sk. W. C for each town negro and Ps. 1 32sk. for each male negro in the country, and to the land treasury Ps. 1 for each town negro and Ps 2 tor each male negro in the country, to be paid thus : Capitation tax not amounting to Ps. 20 immediately on taking up the list, but it Ps. 20 and above that sum, in the manner specified in the ordinance of the 11th November 1776.

The negroes born or dead in the course of the year, are not taxable, but they are notwithstanding to be regularly specified in the list delivered. þÿ All other negroes are taxable, including invalids. Exact lists of the town negroes together with increase or decrease are to tie delivered to the commissioners. In like manner the lists of the estates must be made out with a true specification of the number of acres actually in cane cultivation or prepared for this purpose or in any other cultivation or pasture, the number of acres not used and deemed entirely useless. Oil which occasion is to be observed a letter dated 10th May 1840 from the Royal Board of Commerce ordering : that ail certificates in the last mentioned respect are to be issued on oatii by the Piopueior and two respectable and lor that purpose qualified Burghers in the Quarter, as well as provided with the signature of the Captain oi the Quarter, according to the best ol ins knowledge of the land in question. þÿ 'These certificates must be delivered to the Tax Commission seperate from the tax lists, for together with the Matrieul to be transmitted to Copenhagen. þÿ No certificate will be taken notice ol it banded in alter the closure ol the Matrieul. Furthermore the names of the present owners, (as directed for the towns) together with the names of all the inhabitants without exception, are to be specified on the lists For the convenience of the community, and m order to obtain as much regularity as possible in the tax lists, schemes have been

made printed by the Royal westindia government, which schemes will be delivered gratis for the town ot Christiansled and its Jurisdiction, at the burgher councils Ineassator office, and in Frederiksted and its Jurisdiction at the police ollice of that town. It is a duty incumbent on every owner of a house to announce himself as such, in writing to the commission to prevent any doubt who is to pay the house tux ; and it is further directed, that owners of houses, that have been vacant or untenanted for six months or upwards, and inconsequence thereof are entitled to get a proportional reduction in their taxes, are lor that purpose, to come forward with sufficient proof of their assertion in order to enable the commissioners to observe the

needful in the protocol : in which respect tha Commissioners refer to the royal Governments public ition of 20th October, 1 -<36. li is to be observed, that the commission will receive no tax lists, except they are inade out according to the above mentioned schemes, and every column properly filled up. It is however understood, (hat such lists are not required from owner of houses, who have only to announce themselves as such to the commission, though notoecupyingtheirhouses, as in such cases it will be considered sufficient when they announce themselves as such, together with the names of the persons who occupy the house, in writing to the commissioners. Seperate lists duly signed by the owner or occupier for each house or plantation, is to be delivered to the commission, notwithstanding the concerned individual might own more than one house or plantation. All houses in both towns are to be numbered, and the name of the streets to be placed on both sides of the corner houses, painted with white on black ground or vice versa, in a conspicuous manner, according to Govern r General v: Clausens placard of the 4th January 1777. In case of non compliance with the above, the following fines are to be paid and levied for : Ten Pieces of Eight for every list that is not rendered in due time, it be either in town or country, and proprietors, giving in lists which do not contain the explanations dii acted according to the beforementioned schemes will be subjected to the same fine, as the lists

MEXICO. The outbreak in the capital has had its dav, and the government of Senor Bnstamenle is once more on its legs, though somewhat shaken. The revolution, which commenced on the 15th of July, was brought to n close on the 26tli, alter ten days of fighting and three of negotiation. The bloodshed was horrible ; 80 of the actual belligerents and 400 peaceable inhabitants are said to have been killed 'The negotiations were commenced on the 23d, but not concluded until the 26th, when a convention was agreed to, as follows : Art. 1. The lives, persons, offices, and property (ol the insurgents) are guaranteed, in every sense of the word ; the term offices to be understood as applying to those conferred by the Supreme Government. 2. The general in chief, I ) Gabriel Valencia, oilers in every legal manner possible, to use Ins influence with the general government to procure from Congress a reform of the consitution. 3. All the political events which have occurred from the 1 4th inst. to the present, shall be buried in utter oblivion, þÿ the forces which may have adhered to the plan adopted in this capital on the said loth inst. being included in this convention. 4. A free passport out of the Republic shall be granted to any individual of the persons included in this convention, at his own request, even though an action may be pending against him lor political opinions. 5. The insurgent troops shall retire to such position as 1 1 is Excellency Gen. Gabriel Valencia shall select ; and he shall also de-

signate what general of the insurgents shall command them. The latter will be responsible lor any disorders which mav be committed, and for the fulfilment of the orders which the aforesaid general mav have given. 6. His Excellency the general in chief. Gabriel A alencia, and the generals of his army, pledge their honor before the whole world, to cause this convention to be faithfully and legally fulfilled, in all its parts. 7. This convention will be applicable only to Mexicans. 8. This convention, as soon as it is ratified by the chiefs of both parties, shall he promptly carried into effect, and in order to afford time for its ratification, hostilities shall continue suspended until the morning of the 27th, Mexico, Julv 26th, 1810. In the edifice of the Great Society, 11 þÿo clock at night. A letter in the Journal of Commerce, dated July 28 says that the Federalist troops marched out of the city on the 27th with their weapons, artillery &c It was rumored, however, that instead of giving up their arms at n village designated for that purpose, they fortified themselves on a hill, three leagues from the city. There does not seem to he any stipulation for the surrender of weapons, in the convention. General Urrea had fled, and Farias, the provisional President also.

Tiie Civh, War in Mexico. þÿ Insurrections are not pleasant things to happen, or to read about, especially when one comes to the details of wounds, and blood, and rapine and slaughter. Vet one cannot read of them, generally, without interest, especially when the general narrative is enlivened bv personal anecdotes of þÿ hair breadth þÿ scapes," arid perils bravely encountered or skilfully evaded A very graphic and interesting picture of the recent emeuln in the capital of Mexico is given hv a correspondent of the Richmond Compiler, whose letter we copy almost entire. One cannot help respecting the gallantry of brave old Buslamente, as exhibtled-below. Mexico, July 23, 1810. Mv Dear Sir: þÿ For the last nine davs we have been hi the midst of a þÿrevolution of

TCBimtiNISr<&3 ATI? cannons spitting forth their þÿ iron indignaþÿtion þÿ " ol the death shot hissing from þÿalar þÿ the shock, the shout, the groan of war, and þÿ all the currents ol a heady light On Wednesday, the 15lh inst., a body ot between three and four hundred troops headed by one Col. Montorro, proceeded to the national palace before the break day, surprised of the guard and took tlie President, Gen. Bustumente, prisoner. 1 have learned that the liist intimation he had of his danger was from the captain of the guard, who stated that he had been surprised, and his guard taken prisoners, without being able to toi in, or even fire a gun. The old gentleman (the President) þÿ upon receiving ibis disagreeable intelligence, sprang up, buckled on bis sword, took pistols in ins hand, and telling Ins secretary and one of his aids to follow him, they proceeded to the head of the stairs, and were descending into the court, when they lound their way blocked up by the enemy. They retreated to the flat roof of the palace, whence they saw the extent of their danger. A messenger was despatched to the commandant general, w ith orders to call out the troops. ( 1 he messenger was compelled to descend into the street by means of a rope and jumping some thirty J'eel ) On his arrival lie w as informed tliat the commandant general, Filisola, had gone out, and that while hastening to the quarters of one of the regiments lie had been taken prisoner. The messenger then proceeded to me quaiters ot the Gilt regiment, situated in the soutli east

corner ol the palace ; but found that regiment so completely commanded by the troops of the insurgents, stationed on the roof, that not a man could move without the certainty of being shot. He proceeded to another part of the palace, applied a ladder, and was going up into one of the windows, to report to the President, when he saw about 30 muskets in the act of being tired, levelled at him. He jumped down, ran round to the quartel of Gol. Quintero, the officer commanding the 6th, and consulted with him, who advised him to make his escape. This he did. at imminent liazaid, and finally joined the Government troops. In the mean time the President descended into his apartments, where he encountered Gol. Montorro, a sergeant and live men. The colonel ordered him to surrender. The President replied by giving him a blow with his sword, and was tallowing it up with a thrust, when the soldiers were ordered to lire. He turned to them and said, " Soldiers, do you know me? Will you fire upon your general ?" Then turning again upon the colonel, he ran him out of the room. Presently came Gen. Urrea, who had just been released Irorn prison, arid placed at the head ol tlie insurgents. He approached in the attitude of giving the President an embrace þÿ "Stand back, you ungrateful scoundrel !" said the old man; and rushing at him with his sword, he too bolted out of the door. Another colonel, at the head ot twenty men, then came up. The officer said, " Gen. Buslaincnte, 1 am fighting against vour opinions,

not against you. 1 can never forget that you saved my life when 1 was once condemned to be shot lor a similar offence. 1 am sent here, sir. to guard you as a prisoner; and in doing so, 1 will save you from hurt at the expense of my own þÿblood. The insurgents were immediately joined by Gomez Farias, the acknowledged bead of the Federal party, by the principal politicians and officers entertaining the same sentiments, and by a number of volunteer Eeperos. Gomez Farias was proclaimed President ad interim, and tlie constitution of 1824 declared to be re established.

At the same time that troops were sent to arrest the commandant general, others were sent to the house of the Secretary of War, General Almonte. lie, however, bad got wind of the outbreak þÿ was already mounted before their arrival, and escaped from them and three other parties who attempted to stop him on his way to the citadel. Being there, lie promptly adopted such measures as the occasion demanded, anil, in conjunction witli General Valencia, chief of the stall, and

General Mozo, inspector general of artillery, made his arrangements for an attack upon tlie insurgents. A little after 2 o'clock twelve hundred men, principally cavalry and artillery, under the command ol Gen Valencia, marched from the citadel in the Western part of the city, along the street leading thence to the Caile de Fibutcio. Here they were encountered by a body of Federal infantry, who opened an unexpected fire upon their advanced guard. For a moment there was some contusion. '1 he guns, however, were brought up, and a brisk filing commenced þÿ when the Federalists retreated to the corner of the next street. There they were supported by additional troops and for nearly an hour sustained a sharp action. They then retired to their strotig holds, taking possession of the convent o! San Bernardo, the Deputacion, the Portal de Mercaderes, and the towers of the cathedral, Ironi the tops of which they fired at great advantage. The palace was occupied by the main body of their troops, commanded by Urrea in person. The Government troops took possession of the convents of San Augustin, Capuchinas, Espiritu Santo and Profesa, with their infantry, and planted guns at the corners of the streets Tacuba, San Francisco, Refugio, Capuchinas, Monttrilla and Jesus. You must hear in mind that the houses here, except the churches, are all flat roofed ; that the walls are stone from 2 to 0 feet thick, and the streets are perfectly straight, running at right angels. The pieces stationed at the corners of

Monterilla anil Refugio (12 and 18 pounders) did tremendous execution. The Portal de Mercadeies was literally swept away þÿ the exposed corners ol tlie Deputacion were halteied in þÿ a i id the southwest angle of the palace, inhabited by the President, was bored through and ihiouyh. One ol the bulls passed so near the President, tliat for neat an hour he was deaf in one ear. A constant fire w as kept up on all sides from tlie commencement of the attack until 12 o'clock the next day. Some hours before, the President had been voluntarily released from his imprisonment, by Gomez Farias, and was then at head quarters, when a truce of four hours was asked lor by the Federalists. This was granted ; but in about an hour they were seen barrieadmg the stieets around the palace þÿ whereupon hostilities were immediately commenced About 5 þÿo clock the Federalists requested a conference. Commissioners were appointed on both sides, and the conference was held. The Federalists required that the constitution of 1821 should be recognized; that the President should forthwith resign bis office, submitting to an election by tlie people under it ; and that a President pro tempore should be chosen by the high courts martial and of justice, and the actual Congress. The President answered through his commissioners, that they must surrender at discretion, upon the simply gurauty that their lives should lie spared. The discussion of these conflicting views occupied about four hours, during which time the Federalists came out Ironi the

palace, broke open the stores ol the Parian, which stands on the Plaza, immediately in front of the Portal de Mercaderes, and extracted large quantities of lead and copper, to be used as ammunition. At the breaking up of the conference, the firing commenced anew, and continued with short intermissions until about the same hour the next day, when anothei conference was asked and granted, but resulted in no agreement. '1 he lit ing wasonc.e more commenced, and has continued, more or less interruptedly, ever since. It is now eleven þÿo clock at night, (Thursday.) and after a cessation of several hours, owing to a hard rain, the firing has broken out with renewed violence. When tlie action commenced, I stood looking on an hour or more, during which time 13 men on tlie pail of tlie Government were killed, and many n ore wounded. One of the killed was a brave little lellow belonging to a corps of

4i. J «u>; cadi-ls which had been brought out on the occasion, and placed in the very front rank. They behaved admirably, though perhaps not one of them was over sixteen years of age, and many of them were under twelve. Five were killed at their guns in the course of the night. þÿ The rest were placed on the nzoteo of a lofty building, where they have continued to do duty ever since. After the first twenty-four hours, for two or three days, the general lighting was mere þÿhoy p s lay. The men would stand beliind the corners of the squares, where they were stationed, load Ilnur pieces, pop their heads around, and blaze away, when perhaps there was not a linger of an enemy in sight. At the expiration of that time, they began to erect breast- works of bags of sand ; protected bv which they have since tired more regularly and with greater precision. The unoffending citizens seemed to be the greatest sufferers ; for friend or foe, it made no difference with either party, þÿ all who came in their way were sure to have a volley Several of the most respectable ladies, while standing in their balconies, have been killed by chance balls. It is wonderful how the men sustain themselves under ilieir fatigues. They have now been at their guns nine days. They have had no sleep but such as they could snatch by turns, lying on the stone pavements, and have had little to eat. During tlte day they are exposed to a burning sun, and in the evenings, to tropical rams. And yet, night and day, with occasional intermissions of a few hours, they
have kept up a constant fire of musketry and artillery. The forces of the two parties are nearly equal--about 2.300 each.

RUSSIA. After all the contradictory accounts received, it appears that the Russian expedition against Khiva did not succeed. General Perowski, the commander of the expedition, had arrived at St Petersburgh, and stated that he had succeeded in finding a practicable road, but the excessive cold destroyed his camels, which were his only means of transport The campaign is to be re-opened after the great heats, and hopes are entertained that it will he speedily successful. The Augsburgh Gazette states that Prince Paskewitch is to take command of the Russian armies in the approaching campaign, and that he and the Emperor were to set out for the Black Sea toward the end of July; from these circumstances it is inferred that the campaign is to he one ol gieat magnitude and importance. Central Asia is spoken of as likely to be the theatre ol great events. The Presburg Gazette states that letters from Guizzewo (12 miles from Bucharest), dated the 29th of June, contained an announcement that a Russian army of 150.000 men had marched for Syria. Intelligence of the like effect had reached Constantinople ; and the armies assembled by Russia on the borders of the Black Sea were infinitely more numerous than the pretext for them (the war in Circassia) would justify.

We have frequently had the ungracious task of refuting the false statements of our contemporaries, and it is hardly to be believed that journals which profess to be well informed can hazard such assertions when the daily French press affords the means of refutation. The King of the French. þÿ The recent unequivocal declaration of the King of the French at Boulogne, that he earnestly desires peace, and that whilst he lives there shall be no war between France and England, deprives the proceedings of M. Thiers and his journalists of a good deai of the interest that might otherwise attach to them. Such a pledge, volunteered at such a moment, must, we think, be conclusive ; nor can we understand what there is in the circumstances which appear to have called it forth that is in the slightest degree susceptible of ridicule þÿ His Majesty had just been preserved from a very serious danger, and being unable to suppress what we believe to be his genuine sea timents on the subject of the threatened rupture of France with this country, spoke with the emphasis and deliberation which the importance of the pledge warranted. Nay, not content with having expressed himself in a loud and firm voice in the English language, lie subsequently repeated the same declaration in French. Is it just, or fair, or politic, to doubt the sincerity which inspired it 1 We Confess, we entertain no such doubt. Wg

shall, therefore, for the future, attach much less importance to the demonstration of M. Thiers and the gasconade of the Parisian press than we have been induced to do. We hot only believe that there will be no war, hut are satisfied that M. Thiers never intended to carry the jest farther than would serve jo assist him in the achievement of his own venal objects. As we have niieady remarked, however, the certainty of this fact deprives the future operations of himself and hi# accomplices ol a large proporliou of tliei# importance.

For the Commercial Advertiser. The report of the British commissioners appointed to survey the country connected with the disputed boundary on our North Eastern frontier is a document of great inter est. It gives cause to fear that the settlement of this long vexed and injurious question, is now more distant than ever : it proves indeed the great danger that exists, that it never can be settled by negotiation, and this may well excite alarm in those who view a breach of friendship between the two countries as pregnant with disaster to the interest o! this. Its contents are truly startling; they are at variance with all the documentary evidence hitherto in possession of the government at Washington, or of the authorities of the state of Maine; wiilt all the testimony of suborning American agents, of surveyors and other individuals who have from time to time explored the country ; with all the known maps published in this country or in England, and with the common knowledge of all that part of the population of Maine bordering on the disputed territory ; more especially do they contradict, in essential and well defined particulars, the report of a survey made bv the surveyor general of Gower Canada by order of ihe British government in 1818. I bis latter discrepancy is indeed remarkable. The surveyor general had taken the altitudes of twelve different points in the country he was surveying, and he professes to report these measurements exactly and not through conjecture or by approximation.

The commissioners have visited all these points, and measured the same altitudes by the aid of of scientific means; and they find the report of the surveyor general every in instance erroneous, varying from an error of fifteen hundred feet to one of four hundred. The result of this report are equally striking; they not only substantiate the claim heretofore made by the British government, and assume to prove its justice by the most clear, direct and positive evidence, thus indicating the past ignorance of both governments ns to the features of the country surveyed, but they .fiord ground for the stretching of that claim, over a large and valuable district of country now and ever since its first settlement within the undisputed jurisdiction of the state of Maine. One of the commissioners is a gentleman well known to a large circle of acquaintances >-> the United States. Though English by i iith, he has resided in this country for

Tf> ward of twenty-five years, and continued to reside in this his adopted land up to the day of his receiving this appointment from the British government. For several years past he has styled himself in written documents, þÿ United States Geologist," and though his commission has never been exhibited, yet we must presume that he had one before he could honestly assume to be in the public employ. I am not aware of the reasons that have recommended him to the British government as a fit person to join in this survey ; but now that the report is made and found to be favorable to the pretentions of that government in the premises, it is to be feared that additional force will be given to it from the fact that one of the commissioners is a long resident of this country, a man of science, whose claims to confidence in a business of this nature have been anticipated by the official trust reposed in him by the American government. This question of a disputed boundary, if ever settled amicably, must he settled on the evidence of scientific and competent surveyors. The American people and the members of the English administration cannot repair to the spot and there resolve the problem by inspection, noroan diplomacy at London or Washington determine a question of right, depending as this does on disputed facts. Ihe importance then of this report of commissioners of survey is manifest. It is the ground upon which the British minister will herealier stand ; it is the eye with which his

government will seethe facts of the case ; it is the truth which they will maintain against every contradiction. No one can impute to that government the guilt of the testimony of lying witnesses ; on the contrary, it must he presumed that they have entire faith in the integrity of their own agents, and that they will therefore firmly abide by a report made by those agents, after a personal, scientific arid thorough examination of the country. If this is the case wiih the government, it is likely that the people of Great Britain will have their confidence equally enlisted in favor of this report, and with public sentiment resting on the truth of facts thus ascertained, and inclosing the government as it were with a wall, it is difficult to conceive how an English administration, even if so disposed, can retreat from a ground thus conspicuously assumed. With this view of probable consequences, it is desirable that this report should he met on the threshhold with denial. Long familiarity þÿw ilhthe subject and the evidence heretofore eisting, warrants the assertion of iis falsity in every essential particular ; and the result of the exploration now pro>ecuting by the United States commissioners, will convince the American public of this. In due time it is my intention to enter upon a detailed examination of it, to judge it by iis own face ; by its self contradictions and inconsistencies, its assertions of physical irnposibilities. its unscientific and groundless inferences,

its misstatements of history and its misrepresentations of existing records, to prove it utterly unworthy the credence of all honorable men ; and thus bring into universal and complete discredit a document which if credited by either government or people, must hopelessly embarrass the question, or determine it adversely to the just rights of our own country. AMERICANUS. We differ somewhat from þÿ þÿAmericanus in his estimate of the importance belonging to the report. Having carefully read the whole of it þÿ the þÿ þÿreview as well as the results of the "survey," we are prepared to show that it really adds hut very little strength to the up- > Eiitish claim, even supposing it to go uncon-

tradicted. We find it to he very little more than an elaborate and certainly ingenious attempt to divert the discussion and settlement of the question from the true grounds on which it must be settled Upon those grounds it has very little positive bearing ; and we do not hesitate to say that, so far as the mere question between the two countries is concerned, nine-tenths of the report may be, and must be, set aside altogether, as wholly extransic.

From the New York Commercial Advertiser , September 7, 1840. HANK AND STATE. The Evening Post lately commenced nn editorial article in the following words: þÿ " Now that the National Independent Preasurv bill has become the law of the land --now that the unholy connection heretofore existing between the notional Government and the hanks is dissolved," &.(. Io which we subjoin the following paragraph from the Albany Evening Journal, with some farther illustrations of our own: þÿ . " Divorce of Bank and State." þÿ The public year has been stunned for years with the croakings of the destructives about a < Divorce of bank and state" þÿ and yet, like all their other professions, it is hypocritical and false. Stephen Allen, the independent Treasury receiver, has gone into the Bank of America, where the duties of his office are performed. The parade about " vaults" and safes" was an impudent cheat. The vaults of a bank are used. The business is still done in a bank. The money of the people has been taken from the control otJheir representatives in Congress. The President of the United States is now the President of an ' irredeemable" Treasury bank. On inquiry, we find the preceding statement of the Evening Journal to be substantially true. All the cry about the importance of a " Divokce of Bank and State" is proved to have been false and hollow. I he principles of the Si;b Treasury Bill are enforced just so far as to secure the collection of specie enough to pay the officeholders þÿ just so far as is necessary to keep up such a distinction in the currency as will

secure gold for the house-hold troops, and rags for the people þÿ and no farther. Let a merchant of known responsibility go to the collector to pay a bond, for instance, of a thousand dollars, and present his own check upon the Bank of America tor seven hundred &. fifty dollars þÿ drawn in the ordinary form& another of his own check for the remaining two hundred & titty dollars þÿ adding the words, " in specie and his bond will he given to liirn. Both checks will go to the bank together, be carried through the books together, and the specie drawn upon neither. Or, if drawn, it would only he done in the farcical wav ot counting it out by the paying teller, to be counted in again by the receiving teller, and in thirty minutes he stowed away in the same vault again, where it was before I The Receiver General ketps his office in the bank, and the whole change here, results in the simple (act, that a party favorite has been provided with a snug birth, at four thousand five iiuvdked dollars a year, for doing, or having done, in the Bank of Amorica, what Messrs. Newbold and Thompson did exactly as well, without pay, in the Bank of America þÿbefore! But þÿ in other parts of the Union, where the people and the hanks have not been able to bear up under the cruel policy of t he government as well as they have done in New York, and where the banks have not been able to resume specie payment, the other part of the Sub-Treasury system is in operation Specie is there exacted ; the government and its officers clutch-

ing all the hard money that comes within their grasp, and the rags are literally left for the people. Farther than þÿthis and in all that has been said about a divorce of bank and st;ite> þÿ the Sub-Treasury is sheer imposture.

Melancholy Shipwreck. þÿ The brig Attention, Captain M'Curdy, arrived at this port yesterday, from St. John Newfoundland, and brings advices of the sad shipwreck the of brig Florence, Capt. Samuel Rose, of New York, which vessel left here last spring for Rotterdam, and was on her return passage to New York. The Florence left Rotterdam June 30th, in ballast, and had on board a crew of eight persons, and seventy-nine passengers, men, women and children. After they reached the Bank of Newfoundland, they met with a succession of gales, and foggy, rainy weather. On the morning of the 9th of August, during a thick fog, while going eight or nine knots through the water, she struck on the rocks to the eastward of the Island of Newfoundland, and filled and tell over on her side Immediately a scene of confusion and terror presented itself, the horror of which can better be imagined than described- Here the wife and husband bidding each other a last farewell ; the frantic mother clasping her infant to her bosom, as it even death should not separate them ; and some few who had no relations on board, were endeavoring to secure what money they had, by fastening it to their bodies ; hut which alas, proved the means of their destruction. On attempting to swim to the land, the weight

Capt Rose, with commendable coolness, commanded all to remain by the wreck until some means were devised to escape with safety. For this purpose the second mate, Air. William llobbs, of Spiingfield, Mass. took the end of a line and sprang from the vessel to a ledge which lay between her and the shore ; hut at the time an overwhelming sea overtook him, arid dashed the devoted sailor against the rocks, a mangled corpse. Captain Rose next attempted the only means of saving the fives of those on board. He was more fortunate and reached the land in safety. The crew were all saved, with the exception of the second mate ; but only 30 of the 79 passengers were saved, and of these many were saved by Capt. Rose and the chief mate, Mr. Schofieid at the imminent peril of their own fives. By the time all were on shore who were saved, about three hours after the brig struck, there were scarcely two planks together ; all was literally in splinters. Thus 37 were thrown ashore upon a barren, and to them, an unknown part of the coast. Many were half clad, and most of them without shoes. Not a solitary biscuit was saved. In this pitiable condition they commenced their journey through thick woods and swamps, and over bleak and rugged hills, in hopes of finding some human habitation. For four days they travelled in search of shelter, living upon the hark from the trees, and whatever else oflered itself to satisfy the cravings of hunger. On the 4th day thev reached the village of Kenouse, where they were kindly received and hospi-

table entertained. A Mr Goodrich furnished them with money and clothes, and a vessel to convey them to St John, where they landed on the J 5th There they received every attention which their destitute situation required. Between seventy and eighty pounds sterling were collected, and resolutions were adopted to raise a sum sufficient to enable them to raech their destination especially in the city of New York þÿ The first officer of the Florence reached here on Monday evening in the Attention.

A World's Wonder. The state of things described in the following impressive paragraph, which we copy from the Philadelphia Sentinel, is as true as it is wonderful, and as gratifying as it is true. No other age or country has ever produced, or can now produce, the like of it. " It must certainly be regarded as a most gratifying sign, that with all the excitement which now pervades the country from one end to the other, on the Presidential question, there is little to offend or alarm the lovers of good order, or threaten the security of republicanism. Millions of people are in unrestrained motion, and even ferment. Frequent conventions of zealous partisans, attended by ten, twenty, or forty thousand, and listening for hours, and sometimes days, to the most impassioned, earnest and eloquent orators, are held in all parts of the land, and nearly with as much order and quietness as a Sabbath gathering for religious purposes. No other country in the world could do it. The most stable nations of Europe would reel like a drunkard þÿ would be convulsed with revolution and drenched with blood, in such an experiment upon the populace. Think of such conventions in Paris or London, with all their note of preparation, with all their pageantry, and all their freedom and eloquence of speech, and you think of a revolution. To the enemies of republican forms, the"political agitations of this country may appear precursive of the money sunk them to the bottom. þÿ end. To us, it is the most assuring of its

token of permanence and power, that a great people assembling, as is the wont of ours, like waves or storm clouds, are yet so far the intelligent masters of their passions, that they can deliberate and retire from the most excited gatherings in peace and good temper."

Steamers here, there and every where, þÿ Edinburgh and Hastings at Beyrout þÿ Alecandria, it appears, is at length actually blockaded. Paris, Nov. 1. In the commencement ot the present difference between France arid England, the Parisians were the most warm and excited, and the people of the provinces comparatively calm. A few þÿweeks agitation carried on by the press has altered this state ot things ; the public of Paris remains, indeed, excited but

the provincial French have by degrees been worked up to a state of exasperation and fury- Some few of the departments may form exceptions, but three fourths of them have been made to believe that a new league, like that of Pilriitz, has been formed against France, and that every true Frenchman is called upon to take arms, as he was in 171)3. Substantial causes have come to aid the impulse an J tendency of these ideal and false ones. The alarming and uncertain aspect of politics in general has interrupted every species ot industry, paralysed credit altogeiner. The numbers of the idle and the ruined have greatly increased, and all see in war a game of chance, wtiere more brilliant prizes turn up than in a peaceful course of life. The deputies who have now returned to the capital, breathes all the extra excitement of the provinces; and instead of having their heads and mouths full of local interests, vicinal roads, betroot rail-wavs or coal-mines, they echo the nonsense of the press about the national ling being insulted, the revolution and its interests in danger, and a host of such stock phrases, which evince that however irrational it may he, the French are still highly exasperated and indignant. There is still however, in these a great hesitation as to going to war, they being perfectly aware that none but a revolutionary war is possible, and that the first cannon shot unpins a change of dynasty, as well as a change of political influence and form of government. Anti many a French public man, however

sober and prudent at other times, is at this moment mooting which alternative he should prefer þÿ France humiliating herself be mi a Europe, bv peaceably allowing the lull execution of the Loudon Treaty, or Frame inking every thing throne, freedom dm þÿ influence of the middle þÿclasses -in another thirty yeai þÿs war.

©jisrajE A great man has said, that a great country cannot make a little war. Perhaps this may be contradicted. Perhaps it is one of the great advantage's of G. Britain that it can make a little war, and can employ- force in small and sparing proportions to attain ends not worth an expensive war. Whether this he true or not with regard to England, it is certainly not the case with France. She cannot make a little war. She cannot break over one inch ol her frontier without putting the whole of her neighbors in arms. She dare not menac.e the King of Piedmont without having a million of soldiers ready to resist the armed retaliation of Europe. For this reason, France cannot make other than a revolutionary wart A I Thiers can have no wish to overthrow the dynasty þÿ no wish to transfer the seat of power and influence from the Hall of l)epu. ties to the camp þÿ no wish to see French civilians and their influence turned out at the point of the bayonet in another 18th Brumaire; and vet the proposals which IM. Thiers made to the King the other day, the rejection of which by the King led to his resignation, went to nothing less than such a fearful consummation Thiers was determined to he fully ready for war in spring, if France were still discontented at that time; but France, with a million of men under arms, and the thoughts and interests of her whole population turned to war, must have been discontented with any settlement, and war was inevitable. M. Thiers asked to levy all the French

youths of t wenty years of ago in 1841. calculated at 170.000 men Simultaneously with this levy en masse was to be promulgated a law indefinitely prolonging the period of military service. French soldiers, at present, may be kept seven years in the army though they never aie more than five yeats: but the class ofl8.'f has just been called out and marched in all directions to join their columns in October, wdien they have a legal right to quit them on the 3 1st of of December 1841. It was useless to call them out unless the term of service was prolonged. Now, the prolongation of the term of service instantly operates a revolution in the French army. At present, the youths who join 'he ranks, who scarcely become soldiers for a year or two, and who are to depart at the end of five, do not feel themselves soldiers by profession. Very few of them partake ol the feelings, the inteiests, the ambition, and turbulent excitement of a military life. The present French soldier is a quiet peasant ; hut declare his term of service perpetual, and war becomes his profession and ambition, Levy the entiie youth of the nation, and you will make war the national purpose and ambition. This is what Tliiers wanted to do; and moreover, he proposed collecting immediately this mass of soluiers in camps ofobsei cation on the frontier. Napoleon never issued a more revolutionary or moie despotic decree. No wonder if Prussia took the alarm, and the German States. No wonder that Louis Philippe required time to pause, and liberty

to sec if .till that might be gamed at the risk of war might not yet be gained without it. The new Ministry lias, however, in this undertaken n task of tremendous difficulty. Tiiiuis might have yielded to the Coalition with far more safety than they can He did Mot choose to commit political suicide by

vassaintrass, xatutiKKisr&a ati". doing so; nor can he be altogether blamed. It was too much to ask or expect from any statesman. M Guizot, as a Liberal Con' servalive, is better placed to attempt to reconcile the dignity of France with peace. Will he and Marshal Soul t succeed/ 'Phis is the question asked by every one. Will they have the majority? The loss of M. M. Dufaure and Passy deprive them of some important votes. The discontent of Count Mole þÿ for he is discontented þÿ deprives them of several more. They have, on the other hand, won over the Duke de Broglie, who at first supported M. Tbie/Vs extreme proposals, but w bo now admits their danger. Independent oi all balance enmities or friend ships of individuals, the Souk and Guizot cabinet will have a majoiitv on the addicss þÿ a small majority þÿ a majority which will comprise many indignant and wailike persons, not all prepared to rush into war immediately. Those who will form the complimentary and decisive votes of this majority are members who would have preferred seeing Thiers continue in office and follow up his ordonnances, but who still shrink from lorcin" O Thiers and Barrot on the King with war upon their flag. But, however successful in cam-ins the address and adjourning for a time the great question of peace or war, let it not be supposed that the Cabinet will gather much force from such an achievement. Whether they make peace or menace war, they have still a score of trying parliamentary questions to go through, in any of which they may be

overthrown- Overthrown ! and what is the consequence of the overthrow of the present Cabinet? þÿ7 heconsequence not merelv the accession of the Left (in the person of Thiers and Barrot) to power, but the necessity of an immediate dissolution. It will, and must be, their first, indispensable condition. þÿ Now, there is no one, at all acquainted with the French provinces, who cannot at the instant state the result of a general election within the next year. It would expel from the Chambers all the middle parties, and send deputies of the two extremes into each þÿother presence s þÿ a Mountain and a war party on the one hand, and a herd of halftimid, half furious Conservatives on the other, bent on a policy of rigor and intimidation. As 1 heard a deputy observe not many hours since, þÿ It is not a revolution, arising from an emute in the streets, that is to be feared, but a legal and parliamentary revolution, likely to produce the very same results.

the convocation of the Chambers. All ambition will fail against a monarchy founded and defended by the all-powerful expression of the national will. þÿ The Budget Law will soon he submitted to your examination. 1 have prescribed the most severe economy in the establishment of the ordinary expenses. Events have imposed upon us unexpected charges. 1 have the con. fidence that public prospeiity, at the extreme pitch, will permit us to support them without afleeting the state of our finances. þÿ Other dispositions will he presented to you of public utility on behalf of literature and education. From Belts Weekly Messenger, Nov. 14, 1840. By the arrival of the Indian mail on Wednesday last, it appears that the British naval expedition has arrived m the Chinese waters, and that the operations had partially commenced. The squadron under Sir G Bremier arrived off Canton on the 2lst of June, and that of Admiral Elliott on the 28th. þÿ They immediately proceeded to blockade the port and river of Canton, and to issue a proclamation to the Chinese inhabitants of the sea -coast, that, except so far as such blockade might require, no violence would be exercised upon the persons and properties of the Chinese inhabitants of the sea coast. It is almost needless to observe that the object is to annihilate, for a time, the entire commerce of China, þÿ to intercept the communications from city to city, and thus to create distress both to the government and the people. It appears to be considered that the result of this proceeding will be to excite public discontent in the provinces, and thus to produce pres- a sure on the government which may compel it to acquiesce in our demands. The second measure in contemplation is the occupation of the Island of Chusan, on the north eastern coast of China, an Island about the dimensions of our Isle of Wight, being about twenty-four miles long, and from four to ten miles in breadth, and situate as to one ot the provinces of China as the Isle of Wight is as regards Hampshire. This province, which is culled the Kaing, is about two hundred miles in length, and one hundred and eighty in breadth, and was formerly a resi-

dence of some of the emperors, being one of the most considerable parts of the empire having eleven cities of the first rank, seventvtwo of the third, and eighteen fortresses, and a population of twenty one millions The most immediate question arises, whether this is intended to be a temporary or a permanent occupation. According to the letters from the fleet, the purpose is to take and island, and to retain possession of it until the _ fortify the Chinese government has fully satisfied all our demands. As a means of annoyance and humiliation to the Celestial Empire, as a point J. appui in a war and negotiation, and as an entrepot for commerce, no doubt can he entertained of the utility of such an acquisition.
