My Lord, þÿ Ibraham Pacha having continued since, and not-stunding the defeat of the eoi ps of Osman Pacha, his ... system of dividin' ® fits torces, in order to cover more ground against the projected armaments of the mountaineers, wo have persisted, on our side, to take advantage of his mistakes. On the 8th of October, in the afternoon, General Jochmus occupied the heights of Ardali (where the action of the 2lth of September bad been fougtil) and the village ol Ornaehajuen, without opposition, with a force of four battalions. During the following night about 300 armed peasants joined, and the general made, earlv on the 0th, a reconnaissance on his left to ascertain the nature ot the ground. A skirmish ensued, and the enemy showed about

1500 men, under H assail Bey and Emir Massocd, on the opposite heights of Caiat Meidan. Commodore Napier and Selim Pacha, coming to the heights of Ardali on the 9th, resolved to drive the enemy from his position, in order to facilitate the operations of Emir Beschir Cassim, who having been proclaimed governing prince, in lieu of the old Emir Beschir, had been directed to cross the Kelfason and to enter the provinces above Bevrout : for which purpose he had collected a force of mountaineers, and had been provided with 1 190 muskets for distribution (the fast remaining). The ultimate object of the operation was eventually the taking of Beyrout, whither Admiral Stopford had gone with part of the squadron. The position of the enemy at Caiat Meidan, however, was of prodigious natural stiength, being covered by a deep ravine, and presenting three successive lines of entrenchment; the elevation of the position from the depth of the ravine to the highest redoubt being, peihaps, 1000 yards, and in many parts the rocks were nearly perpendicular. Commodore Napier, with the double view of saving a great loss of life on our part, and of obtaining a greater result in victory, directed General Jochmus to order Omer Bey, who, with five battalions, had been left in our position above Djuni, to march with two of them to Ageltun, there to cross the Ivelhson, and to fall on the enemy in his flank and rear. The Emir Beschir received similar orders. Shortly afterwards, and during the evening of the 9th, we ascer-

tained that Ibrahim Pacha, in person, had arrived at Caiat Meidan with 2000 of his best troops, viz., 1200 Albanian body guards, and 800 of what is called his regular guards. þÿ and his comrades. It is now Perceiving finally his fault, this general had ordered four battalions of Solimau Pacha to join him also, and 2000 more men were approaching from Z ichie, in order to he concentrated in our front. Not a moment was to be lost without compromising the column | of O.ner Bey and the mountaineers of the E nir Beschir. I iie commodore ordered up to the heights of Ardali the three remaining battalions from Djuni, and two Turkish fieldpieces. At two þÿo clock on the 10th of October we had seven battalions at Ardali, when the fire of Outer Bev, approaching by the road of Beohifuya, w as distinctly heard in the þÿenemy rear. s The following dispositions were then taken for an immediate attack One battalion and the mountaineers were directed to cross the ravine which separated us from the enemy,

to Brumana. Four battalions stormed the heights of Caiat Meidan, two in tirailleurs, supported bv two others in close order, moving by the road. Two battalions, reserves, on the heights of Ardali. After two hours' fighting, and the display of the most dating gallantry on the part of the Turks, for the elite troops of the hitherto unvanquished Ibrahim Pacha also stood manfully to their posts, strongly fortified, and facing both attacks, we joined Omer Bey on the heights of Caiat Meidan. The enemy's three lines of retreat being occupied by our respective corps, viz., the road to Brumana hv one column, and the roads to Bechifuya and Corneil by Omer Bey, þÿIbrahim forces s were thrown into the gorge, not 25 men of any of his corps remaining together sunset, and he himself escaping at with difficulty, accompanied by a few horsemen. Eight hundred prisoners, all his stores and ammunition, &c. &c., fell into our hands.

A great many more troops will disperse to their homes, or be pursued by the Etnir Be, chir Cassim, who arrived at sunset withia three þÿhours distance from the field of banle, and communicated to the commodore that he was then observing the 2000 men approach, ing to Ibrahim Pacha s support from Zac,hie. Sn consequence of having been weakened by Ibrahim i acha s order by four battalions. Soiiman Pacha withdrew altogether from Bevrout in the night of the »ih of October, and concentrated in a camp one hour and a half's march east from the town, having the river between himself and the place. The town was consequently occupied by the English and a battalion of Turks on tfie 10th of October, but the news of the entire defeat of Ibrahim Pacha having reached Solimau Pacha's camp, his forces were seized by a panic. He himself, abandoned by his troops, fled in the direction of Damascus, with a few squadrons of horse, and many of his soidters dispersed ; a regiment of 2000 men laid down their arms early on the 1 1th of October at Bevrout, and gave up his entrenched camp, with 19 pieces of artillery, ammunition, stores, &c. Our success has been complete. The Turkish troops fought as they did in the times of Soliman the Great. þÿ To his Excellency Lord Ponsonby, G. C B. &c. dec.

CHINA. We have received, by extraordinary express, accounts from Bombay by the Berenice steamer to the 1st ol October, with dates from China to the 3d of July. The intelligence thus received is of considerable importance, as well in regard to the events which have occurred on our northern frontier in India, as to the operations commenced in the Chinese waters. These operations, up to the last advices, had been limited to the blockade of the river and harbour of Canton, and the departure of the remainder of the fleet from the island of Chusan, in the Eastern sea, not far from the embouchure of the river Yang þÿ'/ sen. The whole of the expedition against China ar. rived there on the 2 lat of June, and on the

V> fallowing- Jiarwutioo, Its inf the 88th as the date when day Sir J. G. Bremer issued a proth® Wtaefcade would commence. The ships fanning the blockade were the Druid, Volage, Hyaonikt, Larne, and the Madagascar steamer. Another attempt had been made by the Chinese to burn the British fleet at Capsingby means of fire-rafts, but it was totally unsuccessful. Previous to this third attempt the Chinese government had sent a boat load; of poisoned tea, packed in smal| parcels, to be sold to the sailors. This nefarious attempt, it is reported, was thus discovtid:þÿ The boat was captured by pirates, who sold her cargo to their fellow countrymen, Many deaths followed the use of the poisoned tea, so many, that it is said the attention of the district magistrates was drawn to the circumstances. On the 28th p. m. Admiral Elliott reached Macao, and proceeded with the superintendent, Captain Elliot, to join the expedition at Chusan. The total British fare® iu the Chinese seas consisted of nine ships of war, throe armed steamers, and twenty transports and troop ships, conveying her Majesty's 49th, 20th and 18lh regiments, the Sepoy volunteers from Calcutta, and a detach meat of sappers and miners from Madras þÿ The whole of the troops were in good health-

Another most important head ol intelligence is the news from Afghanistan and India generally, which is certainly not of a very satisfactory character. It appears that the overtur< s made by Dost Mahomed to Scltah Soojah were but mere pretexts to cover his approach to the frontiers, and it was reported that he had actually succeeded in occasioning an insurrection in Afghanistan, in which Captain Conollv was taken prisoner, and the party accompanying him, cut to pieces hy the rebels. It is also stated, and no doubt appears ot the fact, that one of the rebel princes had attacked the town and fort of Kahun, one of the allies and dependants of the British government. but in the first outset had been repulsed bv the garrison under the command ot Captain Brown. Major Clibborne marched to the relief of the beseiged from Sukkur on the 12th of August, but encountering on the 3lst, in the defile of Poolnjee, a large body of Murrees and Belooehcs, who had destroyed the road and strongly entrenched themselves in the mountains, he was compelled to retreat with a loss of four officers and 250 sepoys killed, as well as of the convoy under his escort. On the receipt of this melancholy news, the Bombay government immediately forwarded reinforcements to Beloochistan, and it was expected that 10,000 men would shortly be in readiness to march against the insurgents þÿ Such is the substance of our Indian news ; the intelligence from China is stated and commented upon in our leading political article

From the St. Thomas Times, Dec. 16, 1840. It is with much pleasure, that we insert in our paper of this day a communication, which has heen addressed to us by an unknown, but, as the writer is pleased to say, þÿ particular þÿfriend þÿofour sand þÿ Well wisher of the Bank of St. Thomas." We beg leave to call the serious attention of all the merchants of this Island to the contents of the same, and return to our þÿ particular þÿfriend our sincere acknowledgments for the atde manner in which he has exposed the baneful consequences, which will result from the severe measure, which our own excellent institution, the Hank of St. Thomas, intends carrying into execution at the commencement of the ensuing year. As we have not for some time past been favored with any thing in the shape of a communication from our subscribers and readers at large, we readily admit this as an earnest, that the lukewarmness which has hitherto characterised our friends on subjects of this nature, has at length given place to a better feeling : we cherish the hope, that should the apprehensions and reasonings of our þÿ particular friend" and þÿ Wellwisher of the Hank of St. þÿThomas, be deemed ungrounded or erroneous, they may elicit a refutation, in the same spirit of moderation which pervades his remarks, from those who view the subject in a different light. We deem it unnecessary to assurearur readers that we shall at all times tenderfhem our hearty co operation, and contribute through the public press to the welfare of our Island, by narrowly watching and pro-

perly exposing those abuses and unwarrantable proceedings, which tend to subvert the commercial prosperity of our little Island. þÿ It is an undeniable fact, and one which we have respectfully unfolded at the foot of the throne of our present Sovereign, that it is only through commerce, unshackled, that St, Thomas can prosper. Our free port, moderate import duties, liberal and protecting commercial laws, our Hanks, Insurance Companies, and the other advantages and facilities which we enjoy and which we know justly to appreciate, þÿ all tend to secure and promote our trade, lhose institutions, which have been established by our liberal and wealthy fellow citizens, on equitable and tried principles, ought not to deviate from the prime ohject, which their founders had in view, when they deliberately laid down their fundamental regulations ; the changes intended to be introduced in them, ought to be minutely canvassed, less they prove injurious to the community which they intended to benefit, and sacrifice the interests they purposed to uphold. When these changes, however, have been adopted, and carried into execution, it is then the duty of every enlightened man, who may deem them injurious, to expose the grounds ol his opinions and to point out the dangerous consequences which will inevitably result from them : it is in this light that we view the object of our þÿfriend scommunication. We seize this opportunity to tender our tribute of re«pect to those, who have been the

founders of our St. Thomas Hank, and we do not flatter them when we say, that we esteem them as men, worthy to be called upon in the furtherance of any institution, either commercial, literary or benevolent, that may tend to promote the worldly interests of their fellowcitizens, or to adorn human Society. Hut although we feel grateful to them for their praise worthy co operation in the establishment of these institutions, we arc impelled on

The object of our Bank is different from that of the Colonial Branch established in this Island ; the latter is guided altogether by interested motives; our's is of a more noble and elevated character ; þÿour i s s to check the arbitrary sway of its rival, to facilitate commercial enterprizes of a legitimate nature, to maintain our exchange wilhm proper bounds, and finally to contribute to the development of our prosperity, without losing sight of its own immediate interests: these should be blended together, for such was the object of its establishment þÿ Without dwelling for the present any longer on the subject, to which we may have subsequently occasion to return, we refer our readers to the communication of our þÿ particular þÿfriend, which will be found in the present publication. -- þÿVIOXiiw M u. Mr. Editor. When an institution, founded by a community, and lustered in its use by die most liberal patronage, to act as a countercheck to a foreign establishment, which thteuieiicd the welfare of that community, loses sight of the main object of its origin, on attaining that degree of power and independance in which it might promote the interest of its founders and ol the public at large; unites hand in hand with that very rival against w Inch it was intended it should act and adopts a system which it was hoped it would not only avert but wholly prevent, even the least interested in it must naturally wonder at so unaccountable a course of conduct, and reflect on the source of that institution, the manner in which it at first corresponded with the expectation ol its movers, its present co-operation with its former rival against its own people) the total frustration of its primitive aim, and the evil consequences which this unpolitical þÿ understanding will produce on the general interest of the public and of the very institution itself. The following þÿ Mr. Editor, is the substance of my allusion. At the time when i( was known that a branch of the Colonial Hank was to be established in this Island, the Merchants, of our tiade, frightened at the inlluence which this þÿ Stranger þÿinstitution, would exercise amongst us, considered it highly indispensable, to recur to some measure that might guard their þÿ money market" from the destructive sway which such immense capital would wield in it, if allowed to

act without a check þÿ its only purport here being to enrich itself. A Hank instituted by the commerce of St: Thomas which should receive the liberal support of this community, and lend in return, a protecting hand against its dreaded rival, was therefore considered as the most effectual countercheck, and, regardless of the individual gain that such an establishment might yield, the main and general advantage to be derived therefrom, which its prospects fully warranted, was that it should keep Exchange and Money within a well regulated value, as also that it should aflord facilities and assistance to its organisers and the trade generally with a becoming remuneration to itself.

Hence, and under such auspices, arose the Hank of St: Thomas : its affairs have hitherto been conducted in a manner which fully realised the anticipations of the public. With a discount of six per cent besides its other traffics, it paid up dividends at the rate of 13 per cent annually, and added once a bonus of 3 per cent, independently of a further reserved fund whie.li exists in the establishment, A more brilliant result never could have I teen expected hv its most sanguine movers, and this was attained while acting up to their intent þÿ This success certainly must be a source of gratification to them, and if that desirable system were persisted in, they would have every reason to applaud themselves, in causing the rise of an institution which so fully compensated their efforts. But it suddenly adopts a course of conduct entirely opposite to that which called for so high an applause, and its future proceedings will apparently baffle the expectations to which the past gave rise. Not satisfied with the prosperous business it has been doing, it desires þÿ to grow þÿricher at the cost of the very trade over which it was intended it should hold a þÿprotector arm. s I.ed hv the influence of the þÿ Stranger Inþÿstitution, the I- ok of St Thomas has given notice, that after the first day of January 1841 its discount will he fixed at 9 per cent per annum Surely when so unreasonable a measure is in agitation, a timely notice mitigiti's the. evil <vhio!i it must produce, but this

pre-meditation of two months does not the less prove, that it is not a scarcity of money that lias given to it a greater value, hut shews a purely moneymaking disposition. It is well known that the needer of money will give £ per cent, additional, and it is natural to conclude, that if the funds of the Hank he as finely employed at that rate as when at 6 per cent, the rates will from the same cause he altered from 9 to 12 per cent as from 6 to 9 per cent. This inctease is but a plain inti ination of the oppression to which the c< mmerce of St. Thomas will be subjected hereafter by its own creature, which yielding to the irresistalde ambition bv which it is directed, will ultimately forget its makers and the þÿ primary and groundwork of its exisþÿtanee. lew would like to he exposed to obtain money at such rates when Tiade is easy, it must affect their credit with the Directors of the Hank severally, who are established merchants of this place, and with whom they may lie engaged in businessthey would then keep hack, although the pur pose for which they niav require funds he a most legitimate one. Hut let us put aside tiles important considerations, and turn our iattention to another, no less to be affected by the menns which we condemn. þÿI heHanks have withdrawn from the merchants the whole of the exchange businesst and therefore rule the commerce of this Island. Il the Hank of 8t. T homos shews the disposition above alluded to, in raising its rates in one way, what shall prevent it from

governing exchange in a proportionally severe manner, by offering such a very low exchange to the Hill holders ns to render the result ol their speculations an unprofitable investment of Capital. þÿ Ibis new conduct adopted by the Hank of fSt. Thomas cannot but rebound to its own disadvantage, and drive business from its doors. The trade of 8t. Thomas is already suffering great inconveniences, and if others are brought on by the very inward source, winch

should strcngihen it in moments of need, little will bo wonting to put an end to the equal continuance of its commerce. By a liberal course, adopted on a correct view of atiairs> an institution like the Bank of St. Thomas, might draw speculators here to raise funds for investments in produce in Pto. Uico, Cuba and the tVI ain, and would also sooner thereby attain its object of securing the hitherto highly satisfactory profits, and, probably, of augmenting them, than by confining itself to profits which cannot but prove momentary. It would then fulfil itsgrand object, thatof equalizing the þÿ money market" and keeping the Colonial Branch in a well beaten path. Mr. Editor þÿ Want of knowledge often leads person, a otherwise indulgent, to regard as errors all reasons which by their wise and elevated nature, are placed beyond his conception in expressing my opinion on the Bank of St. Thomas, I may likely have been labouring under the unhappy influence of ignorance, and 1 may have considered as easy and plain facts, questions which 1 should have respected as inaccessible to my weak judgment. All this can well be the case, but I have formed an opinion, it is perhaps that of many, and 1 have exposed it. þÿ Mv task is done, I must now crave your pardon for having thus trespassed on you, and style myself a wellwisher of the Bank. 10 til December 1840.

Unlawful Marriage. þÿ The town lias been full of rumors for a day or two past, respecting the solemnization of a marriage between parties disabled by the laws of Cod arid man from entering into the estate. We proeure our information from the best sources, and consequently it can be relied upon as correct On Monday morning last, about eleven o'clock, four persons, two males and two females, called at the office of Alderman Campbell, noiiliwest corner of Eighth and Filzwaier streets, and desired that two of them should be married. Those who stepped forward for the purpose, were Mr. James Eneu, said to tie aged eighty-four years, and Miss Emma Haines, said to be aged about twenty. Alderman Campbell made all the legal inquiries parliculuilv, and the more so, because of the disparity in the aacs of the parties. Besides the two, were present a gentleman whom Alderman Campbell knew to be the next door neighbor of Mr. Eneu, and a lady who represented herself as the sister of the bride. To all his interrogatories, they with one accord replied that there was no just impediment. Thus assured, the Alderman could not but proceed, and the Ceremony was performed, and the parties left the office. About nightfall, a person called on Alderman Campbell, and informed him that he bad married a grand lather to his granddaughter; and, on inquiry, this was proved to be the fact, lie felt perfectly free from blame, because he had done all that the law required at his hands, and placed every dependence upon the respectability of those

concerned. The marriage, we are assured, has never been consummated. The mother of the bride, and herself, live in the house of Eneu. On Tuesday, Mr. E. called on the Alderman, and wished him to cancel the Certificate, which was out of his power, but he inquired of him why he had not, informed him ol the disability. Mr. Eneu replied that he was not aware, at the time, of what he now knew : that both the laws of the land and of the church to which he was attached, forbade a contract of marriage between all so allied It is null and void to all intents and purposes I lie above are the facts of the case as they really are, though they arc many things stated by the tongue of rumor which have no foundation þÿ Phil. AS the Advertisement of Assessor Pharmacia; and Apothecary Bbnzon which appeared in last Monday's paper, might, from the lofty words in which it is couched, lead the community to suppose that he had convicted the two physicians therein alluded to, of unfairly injuring his character as an apothecary, and also of unjustly misrepresenting the efficacy of certain remedies two blisters lately obtained from his shop, we have thought it worth while thus publicly to state thai nothing ' of the kind has occurred. A statement of all the circumstances of the case may be found in the protocol of the Notary Public of this jurisdiction Let Mr Bbnzon make the best use of it that he can. We would remind him, however, of the homely adage which assures us that those who seek trouble, are likely to meet with it ; and that, although he may have procured from the Landphysicus a certificate which, he would lead us to believe, perfectly assuages the irritation of his exquisite sensi bility on the present occasion, yet that evidence quite as valid, or more so, may be adduced to prove the inefficiency of his blisters in this, as well as in other instances. New Orleans, Dec. 23, 1840. The cotton crop will be very large, notwithstanding the cry about the worm having committed great ravages upon it. It will, 1 think, exceed 2,000 000 bales. The sugar crop is said also to he remarkably fine, but the production will probably not be as great as that of last year.

Mrs. Kinney, we understand, has remained at the Bromfield House, in this city, since her acquittal, with some of her friends, and has freely conversed with all who have desired to see her, although in a feeble state of health, consequent upon close confinement in prison and the excitement of the trial.
